title: LLM Evaluation
blurb: Tests why accuracy stops applying to generated text, what BLEU and ROUGE measure and miss, LLM-as-judge and its biases, RAGAS-style metrics for retrieval and generation, inter-annotator agreement, and where benchmarks fit.

questions.prompt: Why does classification accuracy stop applying to open-ended generated text?
options: Accuracy only works on numeric outputs, not strings.
There is no single correct output to compare against. Many different answers can be good.
Generated text is too long for accuracy to be computed quickly over a whole test set.
Accuracy needs probabilities, and LLMs don't produce them.
questions.explanation: Accuracy, precision and recall assume one ground-truth label. Two different sentences can both be excellent answers, and a near-copy with one wrong fact can be terrible. LLMs do produce probabilities, but that isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: How do production systems usually combine evaluation methods?
options: BLEU runs on every change, and nothing else is needed.
An LLM judge runs on every change, and human review runs periodically to calibrate it.
Human review runs on every change, and an LLM judge runs once a year to check the humans.
Benchmarks run on every change, since they measure the application.
questions.explanation: Judges are cheap enough for continuous use. Humans are slow and costly, so they calibrate the judge and catch what it misses. BLEU alone is weak, and benchmarks measure general capability, not the application.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say reference metrics and benchmarks are cheap?
options: They are free because their authors maintain them and host the scoring servers.
They run on CPUs, which are cheaper than GPUs.
They measure something next to quality, not quality itself.
They only need one reference answer per question.
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section says cost and reliability move together. The cheap methods are cheap because they measure lexical overlap or general capability, which sit next to the quality you care about.

questions.prompt: What does ROUGE-L measure?
options: Semantic similarity between sentence embeddings
The longest common subsequence between candidate and reference
The share of reference unigrams that also turn up somewhere in the candidate
Precision-weighted n-gram overlap with a brevity penalty
questions.explanation: ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. Unigram overlap is ROUGE-1. The brevity penalty belongs to BLEU. None of these metrics use embeddings, which is their weakness.

questions.prompt: Reference: "the cat sat on the mat" (6 words). Candidate: "a feline was resting on the rug" (7 words). Two words overlap ("on", "the"). What is the ROUGE-1 F1? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Precision = 2/7, recall = 2/6. F1 = 2PR / (P + R) = 4/13 = 0.308. That is the chapter's result for a faithful paraphrase that ROUGE scores low.

questions.prompt: A 9-word reference says a drug "is safe for patients". The candidate repeats all nine words and adds "not". What is the ROUGE-1 F1? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Overlap is 9. Precision = 9/10, recall = 9/9. F1 = 2 × 0.9 × 1 / 1.9 = 0.947. A dangerously wrong answer scores near perfect.

questions.prompt: How should a ROUGE or BLEU score be read, per the chapter?
options: A low score proves poor quality, but a high score says nothing either way about it.
A high score proves quality, and a low score proves poor quality.
A high score is weak evidence of quality, and a low score is no evidence of poor quality.
Neither tells you anything, so they should never be computed.
questions.explanation: The metrics measure lexical overlap, not meaning. A paraphrase can score low and a negation high. They are still cheap and deterministic, which keeps them useful as sanity checks.

questions.prompt: In the verbose restatement, ROUGE-L recall was 0.429 but precision only 0.136. What does that show?
options: The candidate was shorter than the reference, so precision fell as each missing word counted against it.
Most reference words appear in the long candidate, but padding with filler drags precision down.
ROUGE-L can't be computed on texts of different lengths.
The candidate left out most of the reference, so recall fell.
questions.explanation: Recall asks how much of the reference is covered, which is reasonable. Precision asks how much of the candidate matches, which collapses when it is padded. The chapter links this to the verbosity bias of LLM judges.

questions.prompt: In pairwise comparisons, a judge keeps favouring whichever response comes first. Which bias is this?
options: Self-preference bias
Verbosity bias
Position bias
Recency bias in the rubric
questions.explanation: Favouring the first response regardless of quality is position bias. Verbosity bias favours longer answers. Self-preference bias favours outputs from the judge's own model family.

questions.prompt: compare_debiased in Listing 32.2 runs the comparison twice. The first run says "A". The swapped run says "A", which maps back to "B". What does it return?
options: B, because the swapped run is the corrected one
It raises an error, because the verdicts conflict
TIE, because the two orderings disagree
A, because the first run counts most
questions.explanation: The second verdict is mapped back, so "A" in swapped order means response B. The mapped verdicts are A and B, which disagree, so the function returns TIE. It only trusts a winner that survives the swap.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter suggest mitigating self-preference bias?
options: Correlate response length with score after the fact.
Use a judge from a different model family, and check it against human scores now and then.
Score both orderings of every pair and keep only the verdicts that agree.
Ask the judge to be fair in the rubric.
questions.explanation: Self-preference is a judge favouring its own family. A different family and periodic human checks address it. Order-swapping fixes position bias, and length correlation checks for verbosity bias.

questions.prompt: Procedure 32.1's rubric asks for one or two sentences of reasoning before the score. Why?
options: It lets the parser find the score without a fixed format.
It stops the judge from seeing the response twice.
Reasoning first gives steadier, more consistent scores than asking for a bare number.
It makes the judge's output longer, which raises its scores across the board.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake is a bare score with no reasoning, which is noisier. The extra tokens are what steady the judgment. The fixed "SCORE:" line handles parsing.

questions.prompt: length_bias_check in Listing 32.3 reports r = 0.55 between response length and judge score. Longer answers in this set are not better on review. What should the team do?
options: Nothing. A positive correlation proves longer answers are better.
Switch to ROUGE, which has no length effects.
Make every response longer, since the judge prefers longer answers and users never see the scores.
Treat it as verbosity bias, tighten the rubric, and recheck against humans.
questions.explanation: 0.55 is above the listing's 0.3 warning line, and review shows length isn't adding value, so this is verbosity bias. The rubric template already says not to reward length. Recalibrate with humans. ROUGE has its own length problems, as the verbose example showed.

questions.prompt: Which RAGAS metric checks whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context?
options: Context recall
Faithfulness
Answer relevance
Context precision
questions.explanation: Faithfulness catches answers that ignore or go beyond the context, which is hallucination. Answer relevance asks whether the question was addressed. Context precision and recall measure retrieval.

questions.prompt: A RAG answer is wrong. Context recall is high and faithfulness is low. Where is the problem?
options: Generation. Retrieval found what was needed, but the answer wasn't supported by it.
Retrieval. The needed chunks were never fetched.
Neither. The metrics show the answer is fine.
Both. High recall always comes with low faithfulness.
questions.explanation: High recall means retrieval fetched what was needed. Low faithfulness means the answer made claims the context doesn't support. That isolates the generator. Separating the two stages is the point of these metrics.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 32.4 warn against passing the full source document as contexts?
options: Full documents make faithfulness scores negative.
RAGAS should judge what the retriever returned. The full document hides retrieval problems.
It doubles the cost of the answer_relevancy metric.
The ragas library can't read documents longer than 512 tokens, so it truncates them silently.
questions.explanation: Context precision and recall are about the retrieved chunks. Feeding the whole document makes retrieval look perfect by construction, which hides exactly the failures you want to find.

questions.prompt: What does Cohen's kappa measure?
options: The correlation between response length and score
The share of items where both raters independently gave the top score
How closely a judge's scores match ROUGE
Agreement between two raters beyond what chance alone would give
questions.explanation: Kappa corrects raw agreement for chance agreement. If raters disagree a lot, the task is ambiguous or the guidelines unclear, and the scores aren't meaningful.

questions.prompt: Two raters agree on 80% of items. Chance agreement, given their label rates, is 50%. What is Cohen's kappa, (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e)?
questions.explanation: (0.8 − 0.5) / (1 − 0.5) = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6. That is at the chapter's line for generally acceptable.

questions.prompt: Two raters' kappa is 0.35. What does the chapter say to do before using their scores?
options: Average the two raters' scores to cancel out their disagreement.
Use the scores as they are, since any kappa above 0 is useful.
Replace the raters with an LLM judge, which has no agreement problem because it never disagrees with itself.
Write clearer rating guidelines, since below 0.4 the scores don't mean much yet.
questions.explanation: Below 0.4, the chapter says the task needs clearer guidelines before its scores mean anything. Averaging hides the disagreement without fixing it, and judges need human calibration in the first place.

questions.prompt: Which structural limits does the chapter give for benchmark suites like MMLU? Select all that apply.
options: They can only be run by the benchmark's authors
Contamination, when public questions leak into training data
They measure lexical overlap, not meaning
Irrelevance, since a general score says little about a specific application
questions.explanation: The chapter names contamination and irrelevance. Anyone can run public benchmarks. Lexical overlap is the weakness of BLEU and ROUGE.

questions.prompt: A team picks model X over model Y because X scores 4 points higher on MMLU. Their product summarises support tickets. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Ignore all evaluation, since benchmarks and judges are both biased in ways that can't be corrected.
Trust MMLU, since 4 points is a large, reliable gap.
Pick Y, since high benchmark scores usually mean contamination.
Use benchmarks only as a first filter, then evaluate both models on the team's own task.
questions.explanation: Benchmarks are a filter, never a substitute for evaluating the application. MMLU says little about summarising this company's tickets, and the score may be inflated by contamination. A higher score doesn't prove contamination either.

bookExercises.prompt: State the assumption classical evaluation (Chapter 16) depends on, and explain in one sentence why it fails for open-ended text generation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Classical evaluation assumes there is a single correct answer (ground-truth label) to compare a prediction against. This fails for open-ended text generation because two completely different sentences can both be excellent answers, and a nearly-identical sentence can be a terrible answer if it changes one key fact. There is no single string to diff against.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three LLM-judge failure modes covered in Exposition (position, verbosity, self-preference bias) and state the standard mitigation for each.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Position bias: mitigated by scoring both A/B orderings and only trusting a verdict that agrees across both. Verbosity bias: mitigated by explicit "do not reward length" rubric instructions and post-hoc correlation checks between length and score. Self-preference bias: mitigated by using a judge model from a different family than the model(s) being evaluated, validated periodically against human scores.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 32.5's measured results (paraphrase F1=0.308, opposite-meaning F1=0.947), explain concretely why a CI/CD pipeline (Chapter 24) gating deployments purely on "ROUGE score above threshold X" would be dangerous for a model answering medical or safety-related questions.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A ROUGE-threshold gate would have passed the opposite-meaning candidate (F1=0.947, comfortably above almost any reasonable threshold) while potentially failing the faithful paraphrase (F1=0.308, likely below a typical threshold). For a medical or safety-related answering system, this means the gate would happily ship a response that is the factual opposite of correct, and dangerous if acted upon, while blocking a completely correct answer purely because it used different words. The gate would be actively selecting for the wrong outputs, worse than having no automated gate at all in this specific dimension.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the verbose-restatement row's precision (0.136) and recall (0.429) for ROUGE-L, explain in your own words why precision dropped so much further than recall did, and connect this to Procedure 32.3's length-bias check.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Precision dropped further than recall because the verbose candidate contains most of the reference's content (high recall: the reference's words are "found" somewhere in the long candidate) but pads that content with many extra filler words not in the reference (low precision: most of the candidate's own words don't match anything in the reference). This directly mirrors Procedure 32.3's length-bias check. A judge or metric that doesn't specifically penalise unnecessary length will see the high-recall signal and score the verbose answer well, without any correction for the precision cost of all that padding, exactly the mechanism that produces verbosity bias in an LLM judge, just visible here in a purely lexical metric instead.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "we don't need an LLM judge, ROUGE against our reference answers is good enough and it's free." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's Worked Example scored a factually correct paraphrase at 0.308 and a factually opposite, potentially dangerous answer at 0.947 using the exact same reference-based ROUGE metric. The free metric isn't measuring correctness, it's measuring word overlap, and those two things diverge sharply and unpredictably. 'Free' evaluation that ranks a wrong answer above a right one isn't a cost saving. It's a broken signal that would need a second, more reliable method to catch what it misses."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 32.2's `compare_debiased` returns "TIE" whenever the two orderings disagree. Explain what information is lost by collapsing every disagreement into the single label "TIE," and describe one situation where that loss would matter for interpreting evaluation results at scale.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Collapsing "A wins one order, B wins the other" into "TIE" loses the information about *which specific comparisons* were unstable versus genuinely settled. At scale, treating a systematic pattern of position-sensitive disagreement (e.g., always occurring on a particular category of question) as generic noise indistinguishable from a real tie would hide a rubric or judge weakness that's specific to that category, when a closer look might reveal the judge is actually unreliable on a whole class of comparisons rather than randomly inconsistent.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about Cohen's kappa and why it corrects for chance agreement rather than just reporting raw percent agreement. Construct a scenario (two raters, a binary rating task) where percent agreement is high (e.g. 90%) but kappa is low, and explain what that combination reveals about the rating task itself.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Example: two raters rate 100 responses as "helpful" or "not helpful." If 85 of the 100 responses are genuinely helpful and both raters lean toward rating almost everything "helpful" independent of actual quality (say, each rates 90% of responses as helpful), percent agreement can be high (e.g. both say "helpful" on 78 of the 100, both say "not helpful" on 3, giving 81% raw agreement) purely from both raters sharing a strong bias toward the majority label, not from genuine shared judgment on the harder cases. Kappa corrects for this by subtracting out the agreement expected by chance given each rater's marginal label distribution. A low kappa despite high percent agreement reveals that the raters aren't actually discriminating between good and bad responses. They're both just defaulting to the common label most of the time, meaning the task's rating guidelines likely need sharper, more discriminating criteria before the scores are trustworthy.
